questions.q: What does declaring an operation `is Adj + Ctl` actually give you?
options: Faster simulation performance only
Automatic measurement of the qubit at the end of the operation
Permission to call the operation from inside a function
Compiler-generated Adjoint (inverse) and Controlled variants of the operation, without hand-writing either
questions.explain: is Adj + Ctl tells the compiler to generate both the inverse (Adjoint) and the control-gated (Controlled) version of the operation automatically, based on the operation's own body.

questions.q: For the composed operation `EncodeAngle` (Ry(theta) followed by S), what does the compiler-generated Adjoint actually do?
options: Measures the qubit instead of applying any gates
Applies Ry(theta) followed by S again
Applies only Adjoint Ry(theta), ignoring S entirely
Applies Adjoint S first, then Adjoint Ry(theta) -- i.e. reverses the sequence and inverts each step
questions.explain: Correctly inverting a composed sequence of unitary operations requires reversing the order AND inverting each individual step -- the compiler does exactly this automatically rather than you implementing it by hand.

questions.q: Why can't an operation that internally calls `M` (measurement) be declared `is Adj`?
options: Because M can only be used inside functions
Because measurement is not unitary and has no well-defined inverse, so the compiler rejects the Adj claim at compile time
Because M always returns Zero, which breaks the Adjoint functor
Because Adjoint only works on operations with zero qubit parameters
questions.explain: Adjoint requires the operation to be invertible in the unitary sense. Measurement collapses state and discards information irreversibly, so there is no valid inverse -- the compiler checks this and refuses the is Adj declaration rather than generating something incorrect.

questions.q: How does Qiskit's `.inverse()` method on a QuantumCircuit differ from Q#'s Adjoint functor?
options: They are identical in every respect, just different syntax
.inverse() works only on single-qubit gates, while Adjoint works on any operation

.inverse() is a library method operating on already-built circuit objects at the Python level, with no compiler-level guarantee that every custom gate behaves correctly under it; Adjoint is checked and generated by the Q# compiler itself
Qiskit's .inverse() requires re-simulating the circuit, while Q#'s Adjoint does not
questions.explain: Qiskit's inverse()/control() are library-level conveniences composing new circuits from existing ones in Python. Q#'s Adjoint and Controlled are language-level functors the compiler checks and derives directly from the operation's declared characteristics.

options: Applies PrepareSuperposition to q unconditionally, ignoring ctrl
Measures ctrl and discards the result
Returns the Adjoint of PrepareSuperposition instead of the controlled version
Applies PrepareSuperposition to q only if the control qubit ctrl is in the |1> state
questions.explain: The Controlled functor produces a version of the operation that only takes effect when all qubits in the supplied control array -- here, just [ctrl] -- are |1>; otherwise it acts as identity.
